doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Suburban basements and the New Haven jazz scene at Yale
summary: Early playing in basements and a youth wind ensemble, then Yale and New Haven's mid-70s scene with Davis, Lewis, Hemingway, Dresser and others.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: What kind of experiences outside of school in that particular area were you able to find? Because obviously you have to get out and play with people other than just the stage band. Were there opportunities to do that for you?

Yeah, you know, a suburban underground, playing in a lot of basements with friends and jazz groups in suburban basements you know. And I remember joining, forming bands, I remember well geez, let me think about this, I belonged to a Massachusetts Youth Wind Ensemble where I got a lot of interesting experience just playing in a big ensemble. That wasn’t a jazz group per se but invaluable experience learning about what it means to put musicians together to make music. I think my real training ground as a player happened when I got to college, when I was in New Haven. Because that’s when I really started to work playing in clubs and putting on concerts of original music. That’s when it started to happen was really in college.
Were you a music major at Yale?
Yeah I was kind of Liberal Arts, but a music major such as it was.
But you went out of your way to push your own work out there as much as you could.

Yeah. It existed completely. It had nothing to do with the music department. There was a really vibrant jazz scene that was going on in New Haven in the mid-70s. It just happened that a lot of now very highly regarded jazz musicians, you know, and very innovative ones, all happened to be in New Haven at that time.

Oh gee, Anthony Davis, George Lewis, Gerry Hemingway, Mark Dresser, Leo Smith, Bobby Naughton, Mario Pavone. It was an interesting time. These are all very highly regarded jazz artists, and interesting innovative thinkers too, and they all happened to be there at that one time. David Mott — I mean all kinds of people. So there were a lot of

musicians around, a lot of opportunities to play with like-minded players, and we created a scene there, at the clubs and the concert scene. So there was a little burst of activity in New Haven during the 70s. And it was I guess my training ground.
